doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: Exploring, working on weakness, and mentor Ed Clark
summary: Rowe cites Charles Tolliver on 'exploratory'; Griffin recalls Coltrane's advice and Ed Clark telling him to work on his weakness, and tells how he stood up to a bullying cousin.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You make me think of a quote I had set aside here from — I had a session with Charles Tolliver and he kept using the word “exploratory.” And so I finally asked him, well what does that mean? And he said, “Not playing what you practiced that you know is absolutely perfect for the chord changes.”

Yeah. And what you’re describing, being creative and exploratory and looking for new ways, does that tend to sometimes result in something that could be considered unintentional or even called a mistake? And how do you deal with it?

Yeah. Well I can go through some of the things I know some of the masters have said and I started to listen to what they have said. There’s a John Coltrane — a guy said he’d read a book on John Coltrane and John Coltrane, out of reading the book the only thing that he got from the book it said John Coltrane said, he said practice stuff you don’t know. Work on — and then there was a great, great artist friend of mine who probably had the most influential spot in my life was named Ed Clark. Ed Clark was my mentor, my teacher, my best friend, and he just blessed me with so much knowledge and stuff. But he said work on your weakness. Most people fear a runaway or cover-up or figure out ways to not deal with their weakness. And their ego gets into play and you would not let a person know your weakness because you hide them and most of the guys that come across like bullies, they are the weakest person because they are guarding or protecting or sheltering their weakness. So they’re the most probably the most cowardice person in the room comes across as a bully, as the most strongest person. “I can beat you up and I can knock you up.” They are the most afraid and cowardice person. And I experienced that once because my father, my stepfather, he passed away when I was seven years old. And I have a cousin who used to come and he would bully me and he’d take my marbles and you know everything. And one day my dad said, “If you don’t whip his behind I’m going to whip yours.” And so we wrestled, we rustled, we tussled, and somehow he was on top of me and I got the thumb of his finger in my mouth and I nearly bit it off. He didn’t stop crying and running home ‘til he got halfway up the block. From that day on he never, never bullied me or never said anything, and he never, you know made those gestures. That was it. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
